--- title: "Hierarchical clustering" description: "Hierarchical clustering joins stations step by step into a tree that can be cut into any number of groups. How the linkage rule decides what the tree finds, and the adjusted Rand index for comparing two groupings." order: 3 categories: [unsupervised] --- {{< new-terms >}} ## A dendrogram nests groups within groups Groups in data often sit inside larger groups. **Hierarchical clustering** gives every level at once: it builds a tree, the **dendrogram**, which can be cut afterwards into two groups, three, or any number. Benthic survey reports often show one, with hard and soft bottom split first and finer assemblages within each. [Clustering with k-means](clustering.qmd) returns one grouping for one $k$; the tree holds them all. This page builds that tree for the community matrix, shows the one setting that decides what it finds, and introduces a score for how far two groupings agree, which the rest of the section uses to compare clusterings. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the data on this page The coastal survey used here is **simulated**, not a real survey. That is deliberate: because we wrote the generating process (`R/make-example-data.R`), we know the true relationships and can show whether a model recovers them. No real survey is being misrepresented, and the figures are not results about any real species. See `data/README.md` for what is built into it. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the Python tabs Most code blocks on this page have an **R** and a **Python** tab, and picking one switches the whole page. Both run when the site is built, and each tab shows its own output. The Python tab is the scikit-learn equivalent of the R; the figures come from R throughout, and a few steps with no scikit-learn counterpart have no Python tab, which is itself worth noticing. Expect the **numbers to differ slightly** where randomness is involved: R and Python draw their random splits from different generators, so the split is not the same one. The conclusions are. ::: ## The tree records every join of the two closest groups Hierarchical clustering starts with every station in a group of its own. It joins the two closest groups, then the two closest of what remains, and carries on until everything is in one group. The record of those joins is the tree. Each join sits at a height equal to how far apart the two groups were, so a cut across the tree at any height gives a grouping: a high cut gives a few large groups, a lower cut more and smaller ones. ::: {.diagram} ![Hierarchical clustering joins the two closest groups again and again, and records the joins as a tree; cutting the tree at a height gives groups. How far apart two groups are is set by the linkage rule: the nearest members (single), the furthest members (complete), all pairs on average (average), or the rise in the sum of squares if they were joined (Ward).](img/hierarchical-tree.svg){fig-alt="Two cards joined by an arrow, with four small cards below. 1 Join: six points, a to f, in two loose groups; dashed outlines numbered 1 to 4 show the order of joins, a with b first, then d with e, then c joins a and b, then f joins d and e. 2 Cut: the same joins drawn as a tree over the leaves a to f, each join at the height of the distance it bridged; a dashed line high on the tree cuts it into 2 groups, a lower one into 4. Below, under the heading how far apart are two groups, the linkage rule decides, four cards each show a blue and an orange group of three points. Single draws one line between the two nearest members; complete one line between the two furthest; average draws all nine lines between the groups; Ward marks each group's centre and dashed lines from every point to the centre of the two joined, with the caption how much the sum of squares rises if joined."} ::: ## The linkage rule sets the distance between two groups Distance between two stations is the same straight-line distance k-means uses, so the counts need the same log and common scale. Once groups hold more than one station, "closest" needs a rule for the distance between two groups. That rule is the **linkage**: | Linkage | Distance between two groups | | --- | --- | | single | between their two nearest members | | complete | between their two furthest members | | average | averaged over every pair, one member from each group | | Ward | how much the within-cluster sum of squares rises if they are joined | Ward's rule is k-means' own measure, the within-cluster sum of squares, used one join at a time. The others measure plain distances. The four can sound like small variants of one method, but on the same stations they give very different trees. ## Worked example ### One tree holds every number of groups The community matrix and recipe are those of [Clustering with k-means](clustering.qmd). tidyclust's `hier_clust()` takes the linkage; R calls Ward's rule `"ward.D2"`. The tree is fitted once, and `extract_cluster_assignment()` cuts it at whatever number of groups is asked for, here two and three. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} survey <- load_coastal_survey_clean() community <- load_coastal_community() taxa_only <- community |> dplyr::select(starts_with("tax")) cluster_recipe <- recipe(~ ., data = taxa_only) |> step_log(all_numeric_predictors(), offset = 1) |> step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors()) ward_fit <- workflow() |> add_recipe(cluster_recipe) |> add_model(hier_clust(linkage_method = "ward.D2")) |> fit(data = taxa_only) # One tree, cut twice. stations <- community |> mutate(two_groups = extract_cluster_assignment(ward_fit, num_clusters = 2)$.cluster, three_groups = extract_cluster_assignment(ward_fit, num_clusters = 3)$.cluster) |> inner_join(dplyr::select(survey, station_id, depth_m, substrate), by = "station_id") |> mutate(bottom = if_else(substrate %in% c("rock", "gravel"), "hard", "soft")) stations |> summarise(stations = n(), `hard bottom` = sum(bottom == "hard"), `soft bottom` = sum(bottom == "soft"), `median depth (m)` = round(median(depth_m)), .by = c(two_groups, three_groups)) |> arrange(two_groups, three_groups) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|two_groups |three_groups | stations| hard bottom| soft bottom| median depth (m)| |:----------|:------------|--------:|-----------:|-----------:|----------------:| |Cluster_1 |Cluster_1 | 179| 176| 3| 66| |Cluster_2 |Cluster_2 | 394| 14| 380| 118| |Cluster_2 |Cluster_3 | 227| 4| 223| 55|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} import numpy as np import pandas as pd from sklearn.cluster import AgglomerativeClustering from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline from sklearn.preprocessing import FunctionTransformer, StandardScaler from mlbasic_data import load_coastal_community, load_coastal_survey_clean survey = load_coastal_survey_clean() community = load_coastal_community() taxa_only = community.filter(like="tax") cluster_recipe = Pipeline([ ("log", FunctionTransformer(np.log1p, feature_names_out="one-to-one")), ("normalise", StandardScaler()), ]) # scikit-learn cuts the tree as it fits, so each number of groups is one fit. def tree_groups(k, linkage="ward"): model = Pipeline([ ("recipe", cluster_recipe), ("model", AgglomerativeClustering(n_clusters=k, linkage=linkage)), ]).fit(taxa_only) return model["model"].labels_ + 1 stations = community.assign(two_groups=tree_groups(2), three_groups=tree_groups(3)).merge( survey[["station_id", "depth_m", "substrate"]], on="station_id") stations["bottom"] = np.where(stations["substrate"].isin(["rock", "gravel"]), "hard", "soft") (stations.groupby(["two_groups", "three_groups"]) .apply(lambda g: pd.Series({ "stations": len(g), "hard bottom": (g["bottom"] == "hard").sum(), "soft bottom": (g["bottom"] == "soft").sum(), "median depth (m)": round(g["depth_m"].median()), }), include_groups=False) .reset_index()) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | two_groups | three_groups | stations | hard bottom | soft bottom | median depth (m) | |-------------:|---------------:|-----------:|--------------:|--------------:|-------------------:| | 1 | 2 | 394 | 14 | 380 | 118 | | 1 | 3 | 227 | 4 | 223 | 55 | | 2 | 1 | 179 | 176 | 3 | 66 | ::: ::: ::: Cut at two groups, the tree splits the seabed: 176 of the 179 stations in the smaller group are hard bottom, and only 21 stations of 800 sit with the other kind. Cut at three, the hard-bottom group stays whole and the soft-bottom group splits in two, a shallow one of 227 stations (median depth 55 m) and a deep one of 394 (118 m). The groups nest: every group at three is part of one at two. That third group follows depth, which [Clustering with k-means](clustering.qmd) found to be a gradient with no gap in it. A tree will always offer a next split, and the next split can cut a gradient as readily as a real boundary. [Checking a pattern before reporting it](interpreting-patterns.qmd) shows how to tell the two apart. ### The adjusted Rand index shows Ward and k-means nearly agree Ward's two groups look much like k-means' two groups from the first page. A single number for "how alike" makes that precise, and makes it possible to compare any two groupings, including a grouping with the recorded seabed. Take every pair of stations. Two groupings agree about a pair if both put the pair in the same group, or both put it in different groups. The share of pairs they agree about is the **Rand index**. Even two random groupings agree about many pairs, so the **adjusted Rand index** (ARI) subtracts the agreement expected by chance and rescales: - 1 means the groupings are identical. The group numbers do not matter, only which stations are together. - 0 means no more agreement than chance. - The groupings can have different numbers of groups. `adjustedRandIndex()` from the mclust package computes it in R, `adjusted_rand_score()` in scikit-learn. The k-means fit is the one from [Clustering with k-means](clustering.qmd). ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(41) habitat_fit <- workflow() |> add_recipe(cluster_recipe) |> add_model(k_means(num_clusters = 2) |> set_engine("stats", nstart = 25, iter.max = 100)) |> fit(data = taxa_only) kmeans_groups <- extract_cluster_assignment(habitat_fit)$.cluster agreement <- tibble( comparison = c("Ward and k-means", "Ward and recorded seabed", "k-means and recorded seabed"), ARI = c(adjustedRandIndex(stations$two_groups, kmeans_groups), adjustedRandIndex(stations$two_groups, stations$bottom), adjustedRandIndex(kmeans_groups, stations$bottom))) agreement |> mutate(ARI = round(ARI, 3)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|comparison | ARI| |:---------------------------|-----:| |Ward and k-means | 0.935| |Ward and recorded seabed | 0.889| |k-means and recorded seabed | 0.920|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} from sklearn.cluster import KMeans from sklearn.metrics import adjusted_rand_score habitat_fit = Pipeline([ ("recipe", cluster_recipe), ("model", KMeans(n_clusters=2, n_init=25, max_iter=100, random_state=41)), ]).fit(taxa_only) kmeans_groups = habitat_fit["model"].labels_ + 1 agreement = pd.DataFrame({ "comparison": ["Ward and k-means", "Ward and recorded seabed", "k-means and recorded seabed"], "ARI": [adjusted_rand_score(stations["two_groups"], kmeans_groups), adjusted_rand_score(stations["two_groups"], stations["bottom"]), adjusted_rand_score(kmeans_groups, stations["bottom"])], }) agreement.round({"ARI": 3}) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | comparison | ARI | |:----------------------------|------:| | Ward and k-means | 0.935 | | Ward and recorded seabed | 0.889 | | k-means and recorded seabed | 0.92 | ::: ::: ::: Ward and k-means agree almost entirely, with an ARI of 0.94. That is no coincidence: both minimise the within-cluster sum of squares, one join at a time or one centre move at a time. Both match the recorded seabed closely, k-means at 0.92 and Ward at 0.89. ### Linkage decides whether the tree chains or finds the seabed Now the same stations, the same distances and the same recipe, with each of the four linkage rules in turn. Each tree is cut at two to six groups, and each grouping is scored against the recorded seabed with the ARI. The share of stations in the largest group shows what each tree is doing. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} fit_tree <- function(linkage) { workflow() |> add_recipe(cluster_recipe) |> add_model(hier_clust(linkage_method = linkage)) |> fit(data = taxa_only) } trees <- map(c(single = "single", average = "average", complete = "complete", Ward = "ward.D2"), fit_tree) linkages <- expand_grid(linkage = names(trees), k = 2:6) |> mutate(groups = map2(linkage, k, \(linkage, k) extract_cluster_assignment(trees[[linkage]], num_clusters = k)$.cluster), ARI = map_dbl(groups, \(g) adjustedRandIndex(g, stations$bottom)), largest_share = map_dbl(groups, \(g) max(table(g)) / length(g))) |> dplyr::select(-groups) linkages |> dplyr::select(linkage, k, ARI) |> pivot_wider(names_from = k, values_from = ARI, names_prefix = "k = ") |> mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 3))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|linkage | k = 2| k = 3| k = 4| k = 5| k = 6| |:--------|-----:|-----:|-----:|-----:|-----:| |single | 0.005| 0.011| 0.021| 0.026| 0.032| |average | 0.026| 0.287| 0.284| 0.284| 0.279| |complete | 0.332| 0.843| 0.837| 0.381| 0.367| |Ward | 0.889| 0.434| 0.402| 0.252| 0.249|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} rows = [] for linkage in ("single", "average", "complete", "ward"): for k in range(2, 7): groups = tree_groups(k, linkage) rows.append({"linkage": linkage, "k": k, "ARI": adjusted_rand_score(groups, stations["bottom"]), "largest_share": np.bincount(groups).max() / len(groups)}) linkages = pd.DataFrame(rows) (linkages.pivot(index="linkage", columns="k", values="ARI") .add_prefix("k = ") .round(3) .reset_index()) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | linkage | k = 2 | k = 3 | k = 4 | k = 5 | k = 6 | |:----------|--------:|--------:|--------:|--------:|--------:| | average | 0.026 | 0.287 | 0.284 | 0.284 | 0.279 | | complete | 0.332 | 0.843 | 0.837 | 0.381 | 0.367 | | single | 0.005 | 0.011 | 0.021 | 0.026 | 0.032 | | ward | 0.889 | 0.434 | 0.402 | 0.252 | 0.249 | ::: ::: ::: ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} linkage_panel <- function(column, label) { ggplot(linkages, aes(k, .data[[column]], colour = str_to_sentence(linkage))) + geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) + geom_point(size = 2.2) + scale_x_continuous(breaks = 2:6) + labs(x = "number of groups", y = label, colour = NULL) } (linkage_panel("ARI", "ARI with recorded seabed") | linkage_panel("largest_share", "share of stations in largest group")) + plot_layout(guides = "collect") & theme(legend.position = "bottom") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![The same stations and distances under four linkage rules, each tree cut at two to six groups. Left: agreement with the recorded seabed (ARI). Right: the share of stations in the largest group.](hierarchical-clustering_files/figure-html/fig-linkage-1.png){#fig-linkage fig-alt='Two line charts against the number of groups from 2 to 6, one line per linkage rule. Left, the adjusted Rand index against the recorded seabed: Ward is highest at 2 groups, 0.89, then falls; complete is 0.33 at 2 groups and peaks at 0.84 at 3; average stays below 0.3 and single near 0. Right, the share of stations in the largest group: single stays above 99% throughout and average above 92%, while complete and Ward fall as groups are added.' width=1800} ::: ::: ::: **Single linkage finds no groups at all.** At every cut it leaves more than 99% of stations in one group and peels off the rest one or two at a time. This is **chaining**. Single linkage joins two groups as soon as any two of their members are close, so a thread of in-between stations links everything into one. Wherever a gradient runs through the data, such a thread exists. Average linkage chains more slowly, and still holds 92% of stations in one group at six groups. **Complete linkage and Ward both find the seabed**, at different cuts. Ward finds it at two groups, with an ARI of 0.89. Complete linkage's first split sets apart 66 stations, 65 of them hard bottom, so it first divides the hard bottom itself; it reaches the seabed split at 3 groups, scoring 0.84. One table, one set of distances and five numbers of groups gave ARIs from 0.005 to 0.89. The default linkage also differs between toolkits: tidyclust's `hier_clust()` and R's `hclust()` use complete linkage, and scikit-learn uses Ward. When the aim is compact groups, as with k-means, Ward is the rule to ask for, and it is worth setting by name. ## A dendrogram depends on its linkage and never undoes a join A dendrogram looks like a fixed picture of the data, but it records one linkage's joins, and a different linkage gives a different tree from the same stations. Joins are also never undone, so an early poor join stays in every grouping above it. Trees suit surveys of hundreds or a few thousand stations: the method keeps the distance between every pair, 10 GB of memory for 50,000 CTD profiles. ## Key points ::: {.key-points} - **Hierarchical clustering** joins the two closest groups again and again, and records the joins as a tree. Cutting the tree gives any number of groups, and the groups nest. - The **linkage** rule sets the distance between two groups. On the same stations, ARIs against the seabed ran from 0.005 (single) to 0.89 (Ward). - Single and average linkage **chain**, leaving nearly every station in one group. A group that holds almost everything is the sign to look for. - Ward's linkage uses k-means' own measure, and its two groups matched k-means' with an ARI of 0.94. - The **adjusted Rand index** compares two groupings pair by pair: 1 is identical, 0 is chance. ::: ## Try it yourself 1. Cut Ward's tree at four groups with `extract_cluster_assignment(ward_fit, num_clusters = 4)`. Which of the three groups splits, and does the split follow the seabed or depth? 2. Complete linkage cut at 3 groups and Ward cut at two both match the seabed well. Compare them with `adjustedRandIndex()`: how alike are they to each other?
